summary: Defines a file format for exchanging fax-like black and white images over the Internet. It builds on an existing image file format and was published as a standards-track document. It now has historic status.

eli5.summary: A way to save a black and white page, like a fax, in a file so any computer can open it and show the same picture.

questions: black and white image exchange format
what resolution should i use for images
subtitle: TIFF-B format for exchanging black and white documents and fax images

tldr.problem: Organizations wanted a standard way to exchange scanned documents and fax images over the Internet, but had no common file format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies TIFF-B (bi-level TIFF) as the format, with compression using MMR (Modified Modified READ from Group 4 fax), MR, or MH compression, and standard resolutions like 300, 400, or 600 dpi for interoperability.
tldr.outcome: The format became a reference standard for fax image interchange but is Historic as other formats (PDF, TIFF variants, web-based transmission) eventually became more prevalent.

facts.label: Multi-page support
facts.value: Yes, one Image File Directory per page

today: RFC 1314 is Historic. While it provided a valuable standard for image interchange over the Internet, other formats eventually became more prevalent. PDF became the dominant format for document exchange, and email and web-based systems adopted various image and document formats. The RFC remains a reference for TIFF-based fax image handling but is no longer the recommended standard for new systems.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 1314 defines a standard file format for exchanging black and white images over the Internet. The document was created because many organizations were beginning to scan documents and exchange them digitally, but lacked agreement on a standard interchange format.

The images may originate from scanners, fax machines, or software, and may be manipulated by software, communicated via FTP or SMTP, printed by laser printers, or sent to fax machines. The RFC specifies a format that provides uniform transfer of high-quality images at reasonable cost and speed, whether files are generated by scanners, fax machines, or software tools.
sections.eli5: Many companies were trying to send scanned documents over the Internet, but everyone was using different formats. This RFC picks one format everyone should use.

sections.title: Relationship to Fax Standards
sections.content:
The RFC builds on existing fax standards (CCITT Group 3 and Group 4) but decouples the data compression from the transmission protocol. In traditional fax, compression (the way data is squeezed to save space), transmission (sending over phone lines), scanning (reading from paper), and printing (output to paper) are bundled together.

Group 3 (G3) fax uses compression called MH or MR at 204 dpi horizontal and 98 dpi (or 196 dpi in fine mode) vertical. Group 4 (G4) fax uses MMR compression at 400 dpi resolution. The RFC proposes separating the encoding technique from transmission: store the image in a file using fax-style compression, then send it using any Internet method (FTP, SMTP, etc.) rather than being locked to real-time phone line transmission.
sections.eli5: Old fax machines combined several things: how to squeeze the image, how to send it, how to read paper, and how to print. The RFC says: use just the squeezing part, and send files however you want.

sections.title: TIFF File Format Structure
sections.content:
TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) is a framework for encoding images using various compression techniques. The TIFF file begins with a header specifying byte order (Big Endian or Little Endian), a version number (always 42), and the offset to the first Image File Directory (IFD).

Each IFD contains directory entries describing the image data: each entry is 12 bytes and consists of a tag, type, length, and value (or pointer to value). For multiple images (multi-page documents), multiple IFDs chain together, each pointing to the next. Image data is organized as horizontal strips for fast row access, with each strip beginning on a byte boundary. The RFC requires that each page be a single strip to avoid the complexity and re-encoding that multiple strips would require.
sections.eli5: A TIFF file is like a labeled box: it starts by saying which end is which and pointing to a directory of what's inside. The directory lists each piece of the image and where to find it.

sections.title: Compression and Encoding Scheme
sections.content:
Images must be stored as TIFF-B (bi-level), meaning pure black and white with one bit per pixel. The RFC recommends MMR (Modified Modified READ, also called Group 4 compression) because it offers superior compression ratios compared to MH and MR (Group 3 methods). However, images may also be compressed using MH or MR compression, or left uncompressed.

When using MR (two-dimensional Group 3) compression, each strip must begin with an absolute one-dimensional line. When using MMR (Group 4) compression, each strip must be encoded as if it were a separate image. G3-encoded images (MH and MR) should be byte-aligned, meaning extra zero bits are added before each end-of-line marker so every line starts on a byte boundary. The RTC (Return to Control signal) of G3 shall not be included at the end of encoded documents.
sections.eli5: Black and white pictures are compressed (squeezed smaller) using special methods borrowed from fax machines. MMR squeezes better than the others, but all three methods work.

sections.title: Resolution and Interoperability
sections.content:
For maximum interoperability, image resolutions should be one of the standard values: 600, 400, or 300 dpi; or one of the standard Group 3 fax resolutions (98 dpi or 196 dpi vertically and 204 dpi horizontally). The RFC does not require that all implementations support every resolution, but recommends these standard values to ensure that images can be read by diverse systems.

When an image must be converted (for example, from 400 dpi to 300 dpi for printing on a different device), the RFC specifies neither who performs the conversion nor which algorithms should be used. The format accommodates various resolutions to support specialized applications and future technologies.
sections.eli5: Different devices work best at different sharpness levels. The RFC suggests a few popular sharpness values so files work on many devices.

sections.title: Scope and Future Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC specifies a format for monochromatic (black and white) bitmapped images only, though the format itself is flexible enough to support gray-scale or color images in the future. The document makes clear that it does not attempt to define an exchange format for all image types that might be transmitted on the Internet.

The developers recognized that the format may have a limited lifespan as more sophisticated standards like Office Document Architecture (ODA) mature. However, at the time of writing, ODA was not yet sufficiently mature. The RFC is intended to fill the need for a standard interchange format until more advanced standards become available. Images encoded in this format should be automatically mappable to future ODA-based formats, providing a transition path.
sections.eli5: This works for black and white page images now, but the standard was written to easily upgrade when better formats come along.
